title: Four thousand orders, zero real money

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a whole campus playing the stock market, with not one real dollar on the line. That's what happened at ÉTS.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Wait, how does that even work? Everyone just pretends to trade?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Pretty much. It's called paper trading. Students get virtual money, place orders on a platform called MarkÉTS, and compete on leaderboards. It was the first competition of its kind run by AlgoÉTS, the student club where Antoine was president.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it's a game, but with real market thinking.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. Over about four months, players placed 4,154 orders. More than 170 people took part, and the top returns on the leaderboards came close to 60 percent.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a lot of traffic for a student project.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And here's the part Antoine is proud of. The platform was built and maintained by students, and it stayed up more than 99 percent of the time. The team also shipped over 15 new features while the competition was live.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Like changing the engine of a car while the race is on.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nice way to put it. Along the way, six new developers joined, and the club grew to 20 members. ÉTS and FÉRIQUE were partners on the project.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What comes next for the club?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The summary points to more platform work, strategies built with machine learning and AI, and more contests.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is that a student club can run a real, reliable platform and teach trading at the same time.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's it. The full write-up has the numbers and a photo of the crowd at one of the events.
